source_text: Hunc ergo, omissis haereticorum fabulis atque figmentis, deum nouit et ueneratur ecclesia; cui testimonium reddit tam inuisibilium quam etiam uisibilium et semper et tota natura: quem angeli adorant, astra mirantur, maria benedicunt, terrae uerentur, inferna quaeque suspiciunt: quem mens omnis humana sentit, etiam si non exprimit: cuius imperio omnia commouentur, fontes scaturiunt, amnes labuntur, fluctus assurgunt, fetus suos cuncta parturiunt, uenti spirare coguntur, imbres ueniunt, maria commouentur, fecunditates suas cuncta ubique diffundunt. qui peculiarem protoplastis aeternae uitae mundum quendam paradisum in oriente constituit: avdorem uitae plantauit; scientiae boni et mai similiter alteram arborem collocauit; mandatum dedit; sententiam contra delictum statuit; Noe iustissimum de diluui periculis pro merito innocentiae fideique seruauit; Enoch transtulit; in amicitiae societatem Abraham allegit; Isaac protexit; Iacob auxit; Moysen ducem populo praefecit; ingemiscentes filios Israel e iugo seruitutis eripuit; legem scripsit; patrum subolem in terram repromissionis induxit; prophetas spiritu instruxit; et per hos omnes filium suum Christum repromisit; et quando daturum se spoponderat, misit. per quem nobis in notitiam uenire uoluit, et in nos indulgentiae suae sinus largos profudit, egenis et abiectis locupletem spiritum conferendo. et quia ultro et largus et bonus est, ne totus hic orbis auersus gratiae eius fluminibus aresceret, apostolos institutores generis nostri in totum orbem mitti per filium suum uoluit, ut condicio generis humani agnosceret institutorem, et, si sequi maluisset, haberet quem pro deo in suis iam postulationibus patrem diceret. cuius non prouidentia tantummodo singillatim per homines cucurrit aut currit, sed etiam per ipsas urbes et ciuitates, quarum exitus prophetarum uocibus cecinit; immo etiam per ipsum totum orbem, cuius propter incredulitatem exitus, plagas, deminutiones poenasque descripsit. et ne quis non etiam ad minima quaeque dei putaret istam infatigabilem prouidentiam peruenire, ex duobus, inquit dominus, passeribus unus non cadet sine patris uoluntate, sed et capilli capitis uestri omnes numerati sunt; cuius etiam cura et prouidentia Israelitarum non siuit nec uestes consumi, nec uilissima iz pedibus calciamenta deteri, sed nec ipsorum postremum adulescentium captiua sarabara comburi. nec immerito; nam si hic omnia complexus est omnia continens (omnia autem et totum ex singulis constant), pertinget consequenter eius ad usque singula quaeque cura, cuius ad totum, quicquid est, peruenit prouidentia. Hinc est quod et desuper cherubim sedet, id est, praeest super operum suorum uarietatem, subiectis throno eius animalibus prae ceteris principatum tenentibus, cuncta desuper crystallo contegente, id est, caelo omnia operiente: quod in firmamentum de aquarum fluente materia fuerat deo iubente solidatum, ut glacies robusta aquarum terram pridem contegentium diuidens medietatem dorso quodam pondera aquae superioris, corroboratis de gelu uiribus, sustineret. nam et rotae subiacent, tempora scilicet, quibus omnia semper mundi membra uoluuntur talibus pedibus adiectis, quibus non in perpetuum stant ista, sed transeunt. sed et per omnes artus stellata sunt oculis; dei enim opera peruigili obtutu contemplanda sunt. in quorum sinu carbonum medius est ignis; siue quoniam ad igneum diem iudicii mundus iste festinat; siue quoniam omnia opera dei ignea, nec sunt tenebrosa, sed uigent; siue etiam, ne, quia ex terrenis ista fuerant orta principiis, naturaliter de originis suae rigore torperent, addita est omnibus interioris spiritus calida natura, quae frigidis concreta corporibus ad usuram uitae aequalia omnibus libramenta ministraret. hic est igitur currus, secundum Dauid, dei. currus enim, inquit, dei decies milies multtMultiplicatus, id est, innumerus, infinitus, immensus. — sub iugo enim naturalis legis omnibus datae alia quasi frenis reuocata retrahuntur, alia quasi effusis habenis excitata impelluntur. mundum enim istum currum dei cum omnibus et ipsi angeli ducunt et astra; quorum uarios licet meatus, certis tamen legibus uinctos, inspicimus ad metas definiti sibi temporis ducere; ut merito nobis quoque cum apostolo et artificem et opera mirantibus exclamare iam libeat: altitudo diuttiarum sapientiae et scientiae dei, quam inscrutabilia iudicia eius et inuestigabiles uiae eius et reliqua.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, the Church knows and venerates this God, omitting the fables and figments of heretics; to whom testimony is rendered by both invisible and visible things, and by all nature always; whom angels adore, stars marvel at, seas bless, lands reverence, and all things in hell look up to; whom every human mind perceives, even if it does not express it; by whose command all things are moved, fountains gush forth, rivers flow, waves surge, all things give birth to their offspring, winds are forced to breathe, rains come, seas are moved, and all things everywhere diffuse their fertility. Who established a certain paradise, a world of eternal life, in the east for the first-formed humans; planted the tree of life; similarly placed another tree of knowledge of good and evil; gave a command; established a sentence against sin; saved righteous Noah from the dangers of the flood on account of his innocence and faith; transferred Enoch; chose Abraham into the fellowship of friendship; protected Isaac; increased Jacob; appointed Moses as leader of the people; rescued the groaning sons of Israel from the yoke of servitude; wrote the law; led the offspring of the fathers into the land of promise; instructed prophets with the Spirit; and through all these promised his Son Christ; and when he had promised to give him, he sent him. Through whom he wanted us to come to knowledge, and he poured out the large bosom of his indulgence upon us, conferring a rich Spirit upon the needy and afflicted. And because he is spontaneous, generous, and good, he did not want this whole world to dry up, turned away from the rivers of his grace, and therefore he wanted apostles, instructors of our race, to be sent into the whole world through his Son, so that the condition of the human race might recognize its instructor, and if it wished to follow, might have one to call Father in its prayers. Whose providence not only runs or has run through individual humans, but also through cities and states, whose outcomes the voices of prophets have sung; indeed, even through the whole world, whose outcome, plagues, diminutions, and punishments he has described on account of its unbelief. And lest anyone think that this untiring providence of God does not reach even the smallest things, the Lord says: not one of two sparrows falls without the will of the Father, and even the hairs of your head are all numbered; whose care and providence did not allow even the clothes of the Israelites to wear out, nor their sandals, the most worthless things, to deteriorate, nor even the captives' hair to be burned. Not without reason; for if he has embraced and contains all things (and all things and the whole consist of individual things), consequently his care reaches to each individual thing, whose providence extends to the whole, whatever it is. Hence it is that he sits upon the cherubim, that is, he presides over the variety of his works, with animals subject to his throne, holding principality over the rest, and all things are covered with crystal above, that is, the heaven operates over all things: which was solidified in the firmament from the flowing matter of waters by God's command, so that the robust ice of the waters that previously covered the earth might divide the middle, supporting the weight of the upper water with strengthened frozen powers. For also the wheels are underneath, namely the times, by which all the members of the world are always turned with such feet added, by which these things do not stand forever, but pass away. But also through all the parts, they are studded with starry eyes; for the works of God are to be contemplated with vigilant gaze. In whose midst is the fire of coal; either because this world hastens to the fiery day of judgment; or because all the works of God are fiery, and not dark, but vigorous; or also because, lest these things, which arose from earthly principles, might naturally grow cold from the rigor of their origin, the warm nature of the inner Spirit has been added to all, which might minister equal balances to all congealed bodies for the use of life. This, therefore, is the chariot of God, according to David. For he says: the chariot of God is multiplied ten thousand times, that is, innumerable, infinite, immense. — For under the yoke of the natural law, all things that have been given are restrained by certain reins, as it were, and others are driven and impelled by loosened reins. For the angels and the stars lead this world, the chariot of God, with all things; whose various courses, though bound by certain laws, we see leading to the goals of defined time; so that we also, with the apostle, marveling at the artisan and the works, may now exclaim: the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how inscrutable are his judgments and uninvestigable his ways, and the rest.

pass_b_english: The Church knows and worships this God, setting aside the fables and inventions of heretics. Both invisible and visible things, and indeed all of nature at all times, bear witness to him. Angels adore him, the stars marvel at him, the seas bless him, the lands revere him, and everything in hell looks up to him. Every human mind perceives him, even if it does not speak of him. By his command all things are set in motion: fountains gush forth, rivers flow, waves surge, every creature gives birth to its young, winds are compelled to blow, rains fall, seas are stirred, and everywhere all things spread their fertility. He planted a paradise in the east, a world of eternal life, for the first-formed humans; he planted the tree of life and likewise placed the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; he gave a command and fixed a sentence against transgression. He rescued righteous Noah from the dangers of the flood because of his innocence and faith; he transferred Enoch; he called Abraham into the fellowship of friendship; he protected Isaac; he increased Jacob; he appointed Moses as leader of the people; he delivered the groaning sons of Israel from the yoke of slavery; he wrote the law; he brought the offspring of the fathers into the land of promise; he instructed the prophets by the Spirit; and through all these he promised his Son Christ, and when he had promised to give him, he sent him. Through the Son he willed that we should come to knowledge, and he poured out the wide embrace of his mercy upon us, conferring a rich Spirit upon the needy and the afflicted. Because he is generous, bountiful, and good, he did not want this whole world to wither, turned away from the rivers of his grace; therefore he willed that apostles, instructors of our race, be sent into all the world through his Son, so that the human race might recognize its teacher and, if it chose to follow, might have someone to call Father in its prayers. His providence does not only run through individual human beings, but also through cities and nations, whose outcomes the voices of prophets have foretold; indeed, even through the whole world, whose end, plagues, diminutions, and punishments he has described because of its unbelief. And so that no one might think this untiring providence of God does not reach even the smallest things, the Lord says: not one of two sparrows falls without the Father's will, and even all the hairs of your head are numbered (Psalm 68:17). His care and providence did not allow the clothes of the Israelites to wear out, nor their sandals, the most worthless things, to deteriorate, nor even the captives' hair to be burned. Not without reason; for if he embraces and contains all things — and all things and the whole consist of individual parts — then his care consequently reaches each individual thing, since his providence extends to the whole, whatever it is. Therefore he sits upon the cherubim; that is, he presides over the variety of his works, with the living creatures subject to his throne, holding principality over the rest, and all things covered above with crystal — that is, the heaven stretching over all things. The heaven was solidified in the firmament from the flowing matter of waters by God's command, so that the robust ice of the waters that once covered the earth might divide the middle, supporting the weight of the upper waters with strengths reinforced by frost. Wheels also lie beneath — namely, the times — by which all the members of the world are always turned; feet are added to them so that these things do not stand forever, but pass away. And through all their parts they are studded with starry eyes; for the works of God are to be contemplated with a vigilant gaze. In their midst is the fire of coals; either because this world hastens toward the fiery day of judgment, or because all the works of God are fiery and not dark but vigorous, or also because, lest these things, which arose from earthly principles, might naturally grow cold from the rigor of their origin, the warm nature of the inner Spirit has been added to all, providing equal balances for all congealed bodies for the use of life. This, then, is the chariot of God, according to David. For he says: the chariot of God is multiplied ten thousand times, that is, innumerable, infinite, immense. For under the yoke of the natural law given to all, some things are drawn back as if by reins, and others are driven forward as if by loosened reins. Both the angels and the stars guide this world, the chariot of God, with all things; we see their various courses, though bound by certain laws, leading to the goals of their appointed time, so that we too, with the apostle, marveling at the artisan and his works, may well exclaim: the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways, and all the rest.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A preserves the nuances of the Latin clauses, and Pass B provides a fluent English rendering that maintains the theological distinctions and causal relations. Scripture citations (Psalm 68:17) are correctly added to the English text to identify the allusion to the hairs of the head.
